issue: In a criminal case under CIPA, must the government formally invoke the state-secrets privilege through the head of the department with control over the matter (or its political head), as Reynolds requires, or may an agency head decline to invoke it?
provision: Classified Information Procedures Act, 18 U.S.C. App. 3 § 4; United States v. Reynolds, 345 U.S. 1 (1953)

sides.position: The state-secrets privilege requires formal invocation by the head of the department with control over the matter or by its political head, as Reynolds requires, even in CIPA criminal proceedings.
cases: United States v. Aref, 533 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 2008)
United States v. Stewart, 590 F.3d 93 (2d Cir. 2009)
United States v. Alahmedalabdaloklah, No. 18-10435 (9th Cir. 2024)

sides.position: An agency head need not personally invoke the state-secrets privilege in criminal matters under CIPA.
cases: United States v. Rosen, 557 F.3d 192 (4th Cir. 2009)
United States v. El-Mezain, 664 F.3d 467 (5th Cir. 2011)

this_court: The Ninth Circuit requires formal invocation by the department head, following Aref and Reynolds, and excuses the government's noncompliance in this case.
quote: Other circuit courts are divided on this issue.
cite: United States v. Ahmed Alahmedalabdaloklah, No. 18-10435 (9th Cir. 2024)
